In this work, the reasoning above was extended to design a phosphine oxide derivative that has an enhanced hydrogen bonding with the FA ion. Here, we report a bi-functional ink additive Bis(2-oxo-3-oxazolidinyl) phosphinic chloride (BOP-Cl) which contains functional groups that form stable complexes with FA to protect the ammonium proton. Moreover, a phosphinic chloride was chosen to enable a selective reaction with the tin oxide surface which is the electron transport layer used in the regular device structure. The molecule functions as an interfacial and grain boundary passivator, mitigating the acid-base reaction at the perovskite tin oxide interface and impeding cation migration at the grain boundary. Hydrogen bonding between BOP-Cl and FA led Page 19 of 54 DE-EE0009512 Massachusetts Institute of Technology to an enhanced crystallization of the perovskite film and reduced the ion migration and losses, especially at the grain boundaries and surfaces. Consequently, we fabricated solar cells using the configuration FTO/CBD SnO with x oxalic acid/perovskite/ion-modulated spiro-MeOTAD/Au. The champion device reaches a PCE of 25.0% with a V of 1.18 V, J of 25.3mA cm−2, and FF of 83.6% (Figure 2.2a). We fabricated three devices to investigate the impact of different strengths in hydrogen bonding between phosphine oxide derivatives and FA ions on the long-term stability of the device. To verify whether the enhanced hydrogen bonding between the FA and phosphine oxide derivative can help reduce ionic migration and losses, we measured device performance at maximum power point and analyzed their decay under continuous illumination at 1 Sun in N2 at 40-45 °C. During the first 200 hours of MPP tracking, we observed notable differences between the 3 devices. In the device without any phosphine oxide derivatives, we observed an initial burn-in of the efficiency to 90% of its maximum in the first several hours (Figure 2.2d black curve). However, in a device with triphenylphosphine oxide (TPPO), we found the efficiency experienced an initial burn-in but recovered to 99% of its initial value (Figure 2.2d salmon curve).
